And he said, O Lord. I have heard called me to a mighty task in a grave and serious hour. Thou art about to shake all nations and the earth and also heaven, that the things that cannot be shaken may remain. 0 Lord, our Lord, Thou hast stooped to honor me to be Thy servant. No man take this honor upon himself save he that is called of God as was Aaron. Thou hast ordained me Thy messenger to them that are stubborn of heart and hard of hearing. They have U • ' rejected Thee, the Master, and it is not to be expected that they will receive me, the servant.

My God, I shall not waste time deploring my weakness nor my un-fittedness for the work. The responsibility is not mine, but Thine. Thou hast said, "I knew thee-I ordained thee-I sanctified thee,“and Thou hast also said,”Thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak." Who am I to argue with Thee or to call into question Thy sovereign choice? The decision is not mine, but Thine. So be it, Lord; Thy will, not mine, be done.

Well do I know, Thou God of the prophets and the apostles, that as lona as I honor Thee Thou wilt honor me. Help me therefore to take this solemn vow to honor Thee in all mv future life and labors, whether by gain or by loss, by life or by death, and then to keep that vow unbroken while I live.

It is time, O God, for Thee to work, for the enemy has entered into Thy pastures and the sheep are torn and scattered. And false shepherds abound who deny the danger and laugh at the perils which surround Thy Rock. The sheep are deceived by these hirelings and follow them covenant and prayer of a preacher Transcribed by

be a witness to the nations. This of his ordination. After the ehlers hands on him he icithdretc to in the silence, farther in than his with touching loyalty while the wolf closes in to kill and destroy. I beseech Thee, give me sharp eyes to detect the presence of the enemy; give me understanding to distinguish the false friend from the true. Give me vision to see and courage to report what I see faithfully. Make the sick sheep will recognize it and follow Thee.

Lord Jesus, I come to Thee for spiritual preparation. Lav Thy hand upon me. Anoint me with thb oil of the New Testament prophet. Forbid that I should become a religious scribe and thus lose my prophetic calling. Save me from the curse that lies dark across the face of the Amercan clergy, the curse of compromise, of imitation, of professionalism. Save me from the error of judging a church by its size, its popularity or the amount of its yearly offering. Help me to remember that I am a prophet -not a promoter, not a religious manager-but a prophet. Let me never become a slave to crowds. Heal my soul of carnal ambitions and deliver me from the itch for publicity. Save me from bondage to things. Let me not waste my days puttering around the house. Lay Thy terror upon me, O God, and drive me to the place of prayer where I may wrestle with principalities and powers and the rulers of the darkness of this world. Deliver me from overeating and late sleeping. Teach me self-discipline that I may be a good soldier of Jesus Christ.

I accept hard work and small rewards in this life. I ask for no easy place. I shall try to be blind to the little ways that could make my life master. If others seek the smoother path I shall try to take the hard way without judging them too harshly. I shall expect opposition and try to take it quietly when it comes. Or if, as sometimes it falleth out to Thy servants, I should have grateful gifts pressed upon me by Thy kindly people, stand by me then and save me from the blight that often follows. Teach me to use whatever I receive in such manner that it will not injure my soul nor diminish my spiritual power. And if in Thy permissive providence honor should come to me from Thy Church, let me not forget in that hour that I am unworthy of the least of Thy mercies, and that if men knew me as intimately as I know myself they would withhold ~ their honors or bestow them upon j others more worthy to receive them.

And now, O Lord of heaven and earth, I consecrate my remaining days to Thee; let them be many or few, as Thou wilt. Let me stand before the great or minister to the poor and lowly; that choice is not mine, and I would not influence it if I could. I am Thy servant to do Thy will, and that will is sweeter to me than position or riches or fame and, I choose it above all things on earth ] or in heaven.

Though I am chosen of Thee and honored by a high and holy calling, let me never forget that I am but 0 a man of dust and ashes, a man with all the natural faults and passions that plague the race of men. I pray Thee, therefore, mv Saviour and Redeemer. save me from myself and from all the injuries I may do myself while trying to be a blessing to others. Fill me with Thy power by the Holy Spirit, and I will go in Thy strength and tell of Thy righteousness, even Thine only. f will spread abroad the message of redeeming. love while my normal powers endure.
Then, dear Lord, when I am old and weary and too tired to go on, have a place ready for me above, and make me to be numbered with Thy saints in glory everlasting. Amen. Amen.
ROTESTANTISNI these days is becoming more and more union conscious. A number of major organizations are busy trying to unite the many separate communions into one super-organization.

That this new movement within the churches springs from honest motives will hardly be daniel by anyone who wishes to be fair to the facts. Many of the leaders in these movements are men of sterling Christian character, their loyalty to their risen Lord long proved beyond dispute. Charity must forbid us to impeach their motives even if wisdom dictates that we respectfully refuse to follow them.

To some of us it seems that it is not organizational union that we need today but spiritual unity rather. Christen(:loni is so radically divided by differences of doctrine, tradition and church polity that real organizational union can be achieved only at the expense of everything distinctive in the doctrines and b;liefs of the various churches. Church union at its best must require a compromise of positions long held sacred by generations of godly men and women. The achievement of organizational harmony would necessitate the surrender of truths which millions hold dear and the shutting of the eyes to doctrinal idiosyncrasies which other millions feel to be unimportant or actually false.

The history of Christianity shows that power has never followed compromise. Mighty uprushings of moral energy came when men of courage and vision dared to preach what they believed to be the Word of God for their day, asking leave of no one and striving for union only with men of like mind. Some of these may have been a bit narrow, and sometimes we could wish that they had been a little more charitable toward those who did not accept their message. God honored them, nevertheless, not for their faults but for their fearless insistence upon one or another great truth which they felt themselves bound to declare. Their message did not unite existing religious factions. Often it divided them further. But the effect of their preaching was to expose hypocrisy, reveal the unreality of Spiritless Christianity and arouse the sluggish multitudes to the facts of salvation and judgment and sharp immediacy of the kingdom of God.

It is not too much to say that we of these later times owe our knowledge of saving truth to these post-New Testament prophets who came bringing not peace but a sword. They kept alive the evangelistic emphasis which alone can bring men to true salvation.

True unity is the union of the hearts and minds of Spirit-born men and women. Its practical power over the life begins when the individual believer receives the vision of his essential oneness with every member of the household of God on earth and in heaven. With the coming of this blessed illumination there can never again be a feeling of religious exclusiveness. There can be no sense of division from anyone who loves the same Lord and is in-dwelt by the same Spirit. Such a believer knows what he means when he says, "I believe in the holy universal church and in the communion of saints. He takes to his heart the whole family of God and asks from his brethren no further marks of identification thana resemblance to the Father of the family.

The true spiritual unity of believers is not something waiting to be achieved. It is a fact, has been a fact since the Spirit came at Pentecost. We do not wait for the fulfillment of our Lord's words, "That they all may be one.“They are now one. Their oneness is stated thus by Paul:”One body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism and one God." Separation of the members in time does not separate them in fact, nor do geographical distances divide them, nor the various organizational compartments in which they may by force of circumstances have been placed.

It remains for each one of us to feel and practice this unity. And we will be wise also to seek that group which best expresses it in practical common living here on this earth. This must be done in utter humility and self rejection, knowing that God has no favorites among His children and that in His heart of love He holds one group as dear as another. Any feeling that our particular group is superior to others is a spiritual evil more destructive to the sense of unity in the body of Christ than outbroken sin could ever be.

Sectarianism is one of the most noxious ills that can afflict any church or denomination. And remember that denominations and churches are only what their members are. That we love our own church and cherish it is most natural and desirable, but never should we allow a feeling of exclusiveness to enter.

The communion of saints, so dear to our fathers, is a precious doctrine almost wholly unknown to gospel Christians in our day. It should be revived again. The sense of spiritual oneness with the universal Church of God is something so wonderful to the heart and so profitable to the soul that we cannot afford to neglect it much longer.

The American Bible Society distributed 4,727,626 comes of the Scriptures in the United States; the books were circulated in 85 different languages. China led in the circulation abroad, with 963,480 of the total foreign circulation of 8,212,848 comes being distributed. Because of the possibility of the closing of areas which had fallen to the Communists, large quantities were flown to the interior, and others sent by boat to Chungking. The demand continues to be high. It was not possible to make further deliveries to Russia during 1949, although two large shipments have been sent since the war. The Bible Society still stands ready to supply the churches and the people of Russia with as many Russian Scriptures as they can use, and to donate paper, machinery, funds, ctc., to revive Scripture publication in Russian and any of the other twentv-five or more languages spoken in the U.S.S.R.

The highway which leads to this center is marked off in squares with different values. The spinning of a wheel determines the number of squares which may be advanced. But, in addition, certain squares reward the player with an extra spin of the wheel ora direct advance of several squares. Other squares impose a penalty on the unlucky player who stops on them. chapters.t: The Christian Funeral Needs a Reformation
p: We have long been of the opinion that for the blood washed Christian the worst thing about dying is the funeral. Even among gospel Christians the funeral obsequies have degenerated into a gloomy ordeal that leaves everybody miserable for days. The only one not affected by the general heaviness that hangs over every thing is the servant of God who has died and in whose honor the service is held. He has gone where the wicked cease from troubling and the weary be at rest. The minister and the undertaker, however, see to it that those who remain are neither untroubled nor at rest.

An odd contradiction exists here, for dolefulness is just what everybody is trying to avoid. Every effort is made to create the impression that the deceased is not really dead, and that the cemetery is not a graveyard at all but a pleasant park where everything is bright and full of cheer. Strangely enough, in spite of this obvious effort, the average funeral (even the Christian funeral) succeeds only in accenting the presence of death all the more. The dimmed lights, the low music, the smell of cut flowers, the unnatural tones of the minister and his slow march ahead of the coffin all contribute to the feeling of utter futility with which the service is charged.

We can't beat death by setting it to music. The instinct of the human heart is too strong to be cheated by little well-meant attempts to turn an'av its thoughts from the serious business of death and dying. Death is a solemn fact. Only unbelief or the insensibility caused by sin prevent the funeral of an unsaved man from being an agony of terror for his unsaved relatives. The honest minister can bring to the funeral of a lost man no real words of hope for the deceased. For the living there is hope, and the minister may do well to point them to the Saviour, but if he has a proper regard for the sacredness of his office he will not give the living false hope concerning the dead.

The basic spirituality of any group of professed Christians may be discovered by observing the conduct of its advocates when faced with the harsh necessity of death. Where there is abounding gospel assurance among believers the funeral invariably takes on the air of a celebration rather than of a lamentation. Where that assurance is lacking, the whole atmosphere reveals it, how ever bravely the minister may quote, " There is no death, what seems so is transition. Where various ecclesiastical wires are pulled in an effort to secure last minute favors for the departed, where every attempt is made to placate death by timid posturing and ingratiating genuffections, we may be sure that the true gospel light has not shined. For a ransomed man knows how to die without crawling, and ransomed men know how to keep their poise in the presence of death.
The early Methodists enjoyed a degree of spiritual victory that lifted them above sorrow at the passing of their brethren. One of their funeral songs, for instance, ran like this:

> Hosanna to Jesus on high!
The soul of our sister is gone
And clasped in the arms of his loce.
Another song often heard when the Methodists lay away their beloved dead was this:

How inferior the songs we sing today at the graves of our Christian dead. The note of joyous triumph is gone. The whole mood reflects the plaintive hopelessness of paganism. By our conduct at the funeral of those who sleep in Jesus we effectually cancel out the testimony they gave while they lived. It is time for a change.

We share with other believers the hope that for many of us the return of Christ may circumvent death and project us into the Immaculate Presence without the necessity of dying. But if not, then let there be no gloomy faces among the few that gather to pay their last regards. We lived with the Resurrection in our heart and died in the Everlasting Arms. Hosanna! There's no room there for lamentation.
"I have observed, said the old historian,

Christians die well. A Christian can die well because lie is the only one who dares to die at all. The lost man cannot afford to die, and that he must die is his infinite woe. A Christian dares to die because his Saviour has died and risen. Let us renounce paganism at our funerals and die as we lived, like Christians.

History shows clearly enough that true spirituality has never at any time been the possession of the masses. The doctrine ofthe remnant is a large and important doctrine both in the Old Testament and in the New. In any given period since the fall of the human race only a few persons ever discerned the right way or walked in God's law.
God's truth has never been popular. Wherever Christianity becomes popular it is not on its way to die; it has already died.

Popular Judaism slew the prophets and crucified Christ. Popular Christianity killed the Reformers, jailed the Quakers and drove John Wesley into the streets. When it comes to religion the crowds are always wrong. At any time there area few who see. and the rest are blinded. To stand by the truth of God against the current religious vogue is always unpopular and may be downright dangerous.

The historic Church, while she was a hated minority group, had a moral power that made her terrible to evil and invincible before her foes. When the Roman masses, without change of heart, were made Christian by baptism, Christianity gained popularity and lost her spiritual glow. From there she went on to adopt the ways of Rome and to follow her pagan religions. The fish caught the fisherman, and what started out to be the conversion of Rome became finally the conversion of the Church. From that ignominious captivity the Church has never been fully delivered.

Christianity's scramble for popularity today is an unconscious acknowledgment of spiritual decline. Her eager fawning at the feet of the world ' s great is a grief to the Holy Ghost and an embarrassment to the sous of God. The lick-spittle attitude of popular Christian leaders toward the world's celebrities would make such men as Elijah or George Fox sick to the stomach.
Saving truth is a rare treasure, and not inanv in any generation possess it. No man ever found thZ way to God by asking the church member on his way to the social.

Lot was a popular believer. He sat in the gates of Sodom. But when trouble struck, he had to send quick for Abraham to get him out of the jam. And where did they find Abraham? Out on the hillside, far away from the fashionable crowds. It has always been so. For ever)' Elijah there have always been four hundred popular prophets of Baal. For every Noah there is always a vast multitude who will not believe it is going to rain.

We are sent to bless the world, but never are we told to compromise with it. Our glory lies in a spiritual withdrawal from all that builds on 'dust. The bee finds no honey while crawling around the hive. Honey is in the flower far away where there is quiet and peace and the sun and the flowing stream; there the bee must go to find it. The Christian will find slim pickings where professed believers play and pray all in one breath. He may be compelled sometimes to travel alone, or at least to go with the ostracized few. To belong to the despised minority may be the price he must pay for power. But power is cheap at any price.

chapters.t: Satan's News Psychological Warfare Against Foreign Missions
p: The devil hates foreign missions. And from his point of view his hatred is entirely justified.
As Hitler once held most of Europe, and as Stalin now holds the satellite countries, so Satan holds under his despotic control the vast majority of mankind.

Every successful missionary drive is a direct attack upon Satan's occupied territory. Naturally he fights such drives with everything at his command. Each new tribe visited with the gospel constitutes a potential threat to his sovereignty, Consequently every advance on any mission field must be made over his bitter and determined resistance.

But Satan is not the big-bruiser type of fighter. He is a master strategist rather who prefers to fight with the more refined weapons of deception and intrigue. So far as possible he avoids the frontal attack. He chooses the lest violent and more effective method of ideological warfare. And with that weapon he is amazingly successful. As the world's smoothest propagandist, he knows how to lay hold of ideas which have originated among the righteous themselves and by a deft twist of thought to turn them back upon their originators.

Another effective trick used by Satan against God's work is to make sly suggestions of a seemingly ill-nocent nature, get those suggestions accepted by large numbers of good people, and then force them for consistency's sake to draw conclusions not apparent in the original proposition.

The work of foreign missions comes in for Satan's most persistent and most carefully-planned attacks. To retain his present degree of power over men he must keep them in darkness. So, to save his own skin, he must stop the work of missions.

One psychological tactic which since the close of the second World War lie has been using against the work of missions with Ltelfing effect we want here to expose. It is the old trick of intimidation and despair used with a new turn to meet a new sitization. By it he has of late been sabotaging missions by means ostensibly intended to further them.

We'11 come to the point. That the second World War radically altered the international picture and upset long established national patterns is well known to everyone. Some ideals died in the great struggle; others were born into abounding life. Moral attitudes shifted. Iii the long bloody seesaw from 1989 to 1945, and in the reconstruction that followed, certain nations fell and others rose to places of new importance. Primitive races got their first taste of power and used it against those who had long been their overlords. Peoples long dominated by the white man have risen and demanded liberty. This has quite naturally great, affected the foreign missions picture. With the anti-Christian Communists riding high and mighty over vast areas of the world the outlook for missions is in many places becoming dim.

This critical situation we have tried to meet by the most direct conditions and called for immediate stepped-up activity on the foreign mission fields to finish the work while we are still permitted to operate. From various fields we hear the report, "We have but little time. Let us put everything possible into foreign missions while the doors are still open have but three rears, or five years, or ten years at the very most is later than you think." These are not the words of irresponsible men nor of opportunists with some private enterprise to promote. They are rather, in some instances, the serious words of honored men who by sacrifice and long patient toil on the field have earned their right to be heard. And they may be right about the shortness of the time. God knows they may be right.

But at this point Satan enters. That there is a critical emergency he does not try to deny. He admits that the advance of Communism may soon bring to a dead stop the work of missions on certain fields. And he does not attempt to silence the cry, "We have but three years, or "We have but five years." It suits his purpose better to let the alarm go out.

The notion that the work of missions is to be one big push and then the closed door is having a paralyzing effect upon the work. Many young men and women who want to give their lives to foreign missions are prevented from doing so by the belief that there is no use to begin at this late date. "The doors are closing, they reason, and it will require several years to get ready to serve on the foreign field. That time it will all be over. So what's the lise'f

That is probably the most serious effect this new psychology of futility is having upon the work. But it is not the only one. Some experienced missionaries who have served for years on the field are not planning to return after their next furlough. The specter of advancing Communism is taking the heart out of them. The fear of uprisings among primitive tribes is discouraging others. A deep unspoken fear is upon many hearts, or at best a chilling sense of hopelessness. The idea that we must hurry because we have but a short time has definitely backfired. Satan has proved himself a master 451 strategist once more by tricking us into retarding the very work we are trying to advance.

Now, where have our mistakes been made? and what can we do to remedy them? One mistake has been the naive belief that we are able to predict the political future of Asia or Europe or the islands of the sea. For our belief that we have but three or five or ten years to work is based solely upon our own private judgment. Newscasters, the public press, honest but unfounded expectations among Christians concerning Russia or Indo-China or the Philippines: these have been the grounds of our predictions. And a smart devil has used the whole thing to confuse young people, stymie mission boards and discourage efforts generally.

The situation can be cleared up by our coming to ourselves and listening commission to preach the gospel to every creature is still in force, and obviously is to remain in force till "the end of the world. No political developments anywhere on earth can nullify Christ's imperative command. It is not our business to sit back and try to guess the outcome of this or that revolution or political maneuver. Our business is to obey our Lord, to go and keep on going till He sweeps down to call His workers home.
Besides, who knows for certain what effect any war or revolution will have upon Christian missions? Iii 1944 which one of us would have

Uncle Henry rana harness shop in a little western town. Business was not too brisk, which left a lot of time on Henry's hands. Around the town itself there was no place to go and practically nothing to see, so the male section of the town's 250 population, as well as quite a few from the surrounding farms, fell into the habit of dropping in on Henry on off days and evenings just to pass the time of day. So it happened that the harness shop became a sort of poor man's club for the "boys" from far and wide.

Uncle Henry's town had only one small spark of religious life, a tiny church which barely managed to stay alive and never managed to provide anything of interest to anyone but the old ladies and the children. „ „
Spirituality among the boys was rather low.

Not long after that Uncle Henry wrote to say that the the harness shop set. All week long it circulated from one hard hand to another around the shop, and when the end of the week came it was a worn and badly wilted magazine. And religion begin to get into the conversation at the harness shop sessions. The "boys" begin to talk about salvation and the deeper life and foreign missions. It was a new thing for most of them.

Well, there might be more to tell but for one thing. Not long ago Uncle Henry died, and with him died the harness shop and the little men's club. The old building stands silent now; the hum of male voices discussing the in its silence it is trying to tell us something.

Throughout all our great land, and over in friendly neighboring Canada, there are thousands of places answering to Uncle Henry's harness shop. They are spots where men and women and young people gather from time to time without too much to occupy their attention. Such a place, for instance, is the reading room in the Y.M.CA., or the public library, or the corner barber shop or beauty parlor, or the waiting room in the doctor's or dentist's office. Then there is the sun room in the old people's home, the reading room at the vet's hospital or the social room at the T B sanatorium.

Everyone will think instantly of some such gathering place in his town or city. For in spite of television and jet propulsion there are still millions of people who by choice or by the pressure of circumstances kill time by idle talk or by staring out the window. A copy of be the evangel of God sent to bring good tidings.

Another fact should be considered also. There are many Christians who know practically nothing about the ~ great task of world-missions being married forward by v„ such a society as the Alliance. They have simply never had the experience of hearing about the heathen and the command to preach the gospel to all nations. They require only information to become enthusiastic supporters of world missions.

Though we desire to see all the good we can in the various religions of the world we are simply unable to find in the Roman Catholic Church anything to commend it finally to the confidence of Bible-honoring Christians. The Bible and the Roman Church appear to be two different worlds, and these are separated from and, for the most part, diametrically opposed to each other.
One proof among many of the basic contradictions between the Bible and the Catholic Church is their respective teachings concerning Mary, the mother of Jesus.

Moses H. Within, in a recent issue of Bible Tidbits, throws into focus this fundamental difference. He sets forth in deadly parallel the respectful but simple language used by the Bible to describe XIary, and the extravagant honorifics given to her by the Church of Rome.

The Bible refers to Mary in the following language: Marg, Virgin, thou that art highly favored, hand - maid of the Lord, mother of my Lord, Mary thy wife, his mother, mother of Jesus, woman, the womb that bare thee.

Over against this modest list may be set the honorifics invented by the Roman Church: Saint Mary, Holy Alcirll, Most Holy Mary, Blessed Mary, Most Blessed MarY. Virgin of Virgins, Virgin Mother of God, Most Blessed Virgin, I.foly Virgin, Sweet Virgin, Inunaculate Virgin, Euer Virgin, Most Glorious Virgin, Lost Gracious Virgin, Mother of God, Mother of the Word Incarnate, Mother of Mercy, Our Lord, Lady in Heaven, Queen of the World, Advocate of Sinners, Dispenser of Divine Grace, Door of Heaven, Intercessor, Madonna, Mediator, Mom ing Star, Protectoress.

To check the accuracy of these lists one need 0111)' read the New Testament and almost any doctrinal or devotional work by a Roman Catholic. It is quite obvious that there are two Niarys before us, the plain meek woman of the Bible and the synthetic "Queen of Heaven created by the Roman Church.

Little comment is indicated. Our Lord said, "But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men. And again he said, " Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered." That just about wraps the matter up for us.

Then Philip preached Christ at Samaria "unclean spirits, crying with were possessed with them." Unclean spirits were obviously those which incited the persons in whom they dwelt to acts of filthiness. Unclean conduct must always have a spiritual origin. The Bible teaches the spiritual basis of morals. The physical body is the obedient servant of the personality that inhabits it, whether that personality be good or evil.

Any true work of God will deal with the unclean spirits of society. The gospel goes to the roots of conduct and makes its transforming changes there. Only a spiritual change can guarantee a permanent reformation in the life. For that reason it is of utmost importance that a revival of transforming grace should begin deep in the hearts of men.

The temptation among revivalists these days is to promote religion by compromising the truth and playing down the need for that more radical change which is demanded in the very nature of things. Instead of casting out the unclean spirits we are prone to whitewash them. Evil spirits which have been partly converted are as certainly damned as are the angels which kept not their first estate and are now reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.

Nien of the world must agree to have their unclean spirits expelled or they can have no sound reason to hope in the gospel. Weak.acceptance" of Christ is not enough. There must be some genuine exorcising of the evil spirits which have been fouling up the springs of life. And there must be a courageous coming out fi-om the company of those who run 4LGOT 12, 1950 in the way of evil. On these two points modern evangelism fails dis-inally. In our eagerness to make converts we have sold the gospel message down river and by compromise and addition we have made it something it is not and has never been. It is time we repent and do our first works again.

Among many that might be cited is one example of moral white-washing which was highlighted recently in a midwestern city. A young actress from Hollywood was invited to address a gathering of religious persons. During her talk she told of her conversion to Christ asa result of the preaching of a certain pastor in her city. Her testimony sounded real and from every appearance she was perfectly sincere in what she said. Then in an outburst of loyalty she suddenly cried, "Some of the most devoted Christians I know are among the actors and actresses in Hollywood." With nothing but complete sympathy for the young woman let us examine this a bit.

I think it will be agreed by all Bible-loving Christians that the moving picture industry represents the distilled quintessence of everything that is worldly and unregenerate. The worst that can be said about it could not be printed in a religious journal and the best can only be described' in the language of the Bible, "Vanity of vanities; all is vanity.

Take a good look at Hollywood and several features will stand out plain as the mountains that rise above the level plain. For one thing, the whole industry is dedicated to a brand of extravagant living which is condemned on every page of the sacred Scriptures. Compare its gilded and expensively attired women with Sarah or Hannah or Dorcas or Susannah Wesley. The contrast may well make you sick. Then Hollywood accepts this world as final and makes no allowance for any other. She considers success in pictures to be the highest good that can come to men and women in this life. Its devotees walk not as strangers and pilgrims but as eager citizens of Vanity Fair, happy and content to be a part of it all. However piously the movie producers may protest, the sum of Hollywood philosophy is that men are made for their appetites and that there is no higher enjoyment shall the pleasures of the flesh. Worse than this is that Fragrant rebellion against the teachings of Christ concerning marriage and the sanctity of the home, Serious students of the over-all special picture may have reason to lay at the feet of the motion picture industry most of the blame for the breakdown of family life so evident in this country in the last half century.

If there are some true Christians associated with the movie industry then we have a perfect right to ask, What are they doing there? A man claiming to be a loyal American habitually marches in communistic parades and frequents communistic meetings. If he is indeed a loyal American what is he doing among the enemies of his country? A man claims to be a law-abiding citizen but hangs out in the back room of a pool hall where gangsters and procurers gather and crimes are planned by men of the underworld. If he is a good citizen what is he doing there?

A woman claims to be a follower of Christ but she plays in pictures and makes herself a part of the pretense and the insincerity and the extravagance and the hollowness and the fleshly display which is Hollywood. If she is a Christian what is she doing there? Unless she c an answer that question satisfactorily *she has no moral right to speak in the holy name of Christ.

No, one of the first things a returning sinner must do is to return. He cannot prove his moral sincerity by staying on in the old haunts. The blessed man standeth (not) in the way of sinners. nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful."

Hollywood is only one example among many. Wherever in the far country the pigsty may be located the prodigal must quit it and travel home if he would wear the new robe and taste the joy of his father's forgiveness. We dare not soft-pedal this truth for fear of offending. Rather we must face up to it boldly and take the consequences.

When the unclean spirits were cast out they came out crying with loud voices. Those eries were eries of frustration and helpless rage. They wanted to stay inside their victims and continue to poison the springs of their lives as they had done before. They went out only under bitter protest. IIad they had access to an organ like the newspaper or the radio they might have made a good case for themselves and proved that they were not unclean at all, but

chapters.t: Reaping the Results of Bad Religious Philosophy
p: WE ARE now- reaping the results of a generation of bad religious philosophy. That philosophy, which might be called "Amateurism, came into Bower half a hundred years ago and is now in full fruit. And to all who love the Church of God the fruit seems wormy and of a bitter taste.

About the time of the incoming of the twentieth century, the signiftcant phenomenon which we name "Amateurism" appeared. It hardly deserves to be called a movement. since it was never organized, sprang from no one source and owed its origin to no single person. It is a ~pint rather thana movement and can best be identified by its characteristic philosophical pattern and the outworking of that philosophy.

By "Amateurism we mean a religious philosophy, based loosely iron the Christian Faith. but containing innumerable admixtures of notions altogether different from and often opposed to the religion of the New Testament. The best way to identify it is to describe it, though its beliefs are so chaotic as host to defy description. The various tenets of its disorderly creed are easily appraised by nothing their issue into practical living.

If the word philosophy would seem a bit too elevated to describe the loose and badly organized thinking back of the creed of Amateurism we would explain that we use the word to indicate the total of what a man believes about any particular thing. Thus understood the word will be quite appropriate.

It is not at all likely that the devotees of Aliiateurism have ever paused to think am'thing through or to discover just what they do believe. Analysis, however. discloses that they have certain views, and these views determine the whole color and tone of their life and worship.

First, in their view the unity of the Church of Christ is altogether ignored. The text "Where two or three are gathered" is misunderstood and used to secure divine sanction for acts which give rein to carnal ambition, gratify the flesh and divide the brethren, allowing any lit-tie badlv-taught group anywhere to set itself up as the very Church of the Living God. Leaders of these isolated groups, though wholly unrelated to any larger body and totally unaware of their place in the divine plan. nevertheless do not hesitate to perform those offices which by scriptural right belong to specially called and Spirit-gifted Inell.

The fact that the members of the Church of Christ are all part of one body and thus dependent upon each other is wholly foreign to the thinking of these brethren. They scorn authority and claim for themselves the right to carry on after their own private whims. Often (though not always) the pastor runs the whole affair. l Ie makes all appointments, counts the money and signs the checks, apparently unaware-that by so doing he destroys public confidence and arouses suspicion of fraud even when the man himself is as honest as daylight.

The spirit of Amateurism ignores the teachings of history. eries down the past, glorifies ignorance, magnifies the coarse and the ugly. caters to low tastes and pals along with any religious nlinstrel who may chance to come along for a one-night stand. Amateurism provides a per-feet atmosphere for the growth of religious racketeers and seems never to get quite free from the tabloid mentality.

In the public services perhaps more than anywhere else the fleshly quality of the whole thing is best seen. The general air is bold and glassy, the service itself badly ordered and artificially stimulated. There Amateurism runs wild. The place becomes a dumping ground for converted third-rate opera stars and broken-down ex-actors who at their best never had more thana walk-on bit part in a class B movie and couldn't hold on to that. But the poor mistaught crowds, with pitiable want of discernment, accept the world's leavings and give them places of prominence in an organization ostensibly dedicated to things heavenly.

The victims of the spirit of Aniateurism, for all their claim to the Spirit's guidance, are vet easy marks for any miracle peddler who hoves into sight. That he has upon him no fragrance of sweet humility or lik{mess to Christ seems not to matter. That he comes with a badly besmirched escutcheon, and with no proof of any subsequent repentance, is blindly overlooked by these friends who accord their hero a degree of generation second onk- to that afforded the saints by the devotees of Rome.

Perhaps the most tragic thing about all this is that miny good people have come to identify Amateurism with the Faith of our Fathers and innocently believe that they are one and the same. Their on-h' contact with the gospel has been in such services as we have here described. They have known nothing else except, perhaps, some watered-down form of religion which failed to present the way of salvation, and the little wisps of real truth they received in the new fellowship came like manna from heaven. The mistake is thus easy enough to understand. butt it is unfortunate nevertheless. For Amateurism is not equal to evangelicalism, though the two are often found in close association. The Full Gospel has run in this wild pasture also and has been falsely identified with it. But the coarse holiness we have described bears nob remote resemblance to the Spirit-filled Christianity of the New Testament. nor to the religion of the Moravians and the Wesleys, nor to the tender beauty of the saints. Protestant Amateurism is altogether incapable of creating such a hymnody as that of the Moravians, the Scotch Presbyterians or the early Methodists. And may we add, it could never give to the Church such a book as Simpson's Hymns of the Christian Life. One has but to listen to the songs of a people to learn the quality of their minds. The singing of those Christians associated with Amateurism is sufficient commentary on their religion.

iVhat shall we do about all this? The ohly defense against the evil is a reverent espousal of the way of Christ and His apostles. Continue, if we will, to worship in simple tabernacles. But keep the building out of our hearts and out of our worship. Bring to our plain buildings all the sweet humility and lofty dignity of true sous and daughters of the new creation. And finally, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.

By returning and rest we may yet be saved, and may find again the spirit of meekness, of gentleness, of reverence which has of late so largely escaped us. And perhaps we may bring again to our churches the beauty that once characterized the followers of the King of all beauty.

chapters.t: "I Believe in the Communion of Saints"
p: Without doubt the most important body on earth is the Church of God which He purchased with His own blood.
Unfortunately the word "church" itself has taken on meanings which it did not originally have and has suffered untold injury in the house both of its enemies and of its friends.
The meaning of the word for the true Christian was fixed by our Lord and His apostles. What they meant by it is what we must mean by it; and no man and no angel has authority to change it.

The simple etymological meaning is easy to discover, but its larger significance must be learned from the New Testament Scriptures. All that is meant by that wondrous word cannot be stated in one sentence, nor in one paragraph, nor scarcely in one book.
The universal Church is the body of Christ, the bride of the Lamb, the habitation of God through the Spirit, the pillar and ground of the truth.

The local church is a community of ransomed men, a minority group, a colony of heavenly souls dwelling apart on the earth, a division of soldiers on a foreign soil, a band of reapers, working under the direction of the Lord of the harvest. a flock of sheep following the Good Shepherd, a brotherhood of like-minded men, a visible representative of the Invisible God.
It is most undesirable to conceive of our churches „ be used, as "Works,“or”Projects. If such words must

then let them be understood as referring to the earthly and legal aspect of things only. A true church is something supernatural and divine, and is in direct lineal descent from that first church at Jerusalem. Insofar as it is a church it is spiritual; its social aspect is secondary and may be imitated by any group regardless of its religious qualities or lack of them. The spiritual essence of a true church cannot be reproduced anywhere but in a company of renewed and inwardly-united believers.

The Christian life begins with the individual; a soul has a saving encounter with God and the new life is born. Not all the pooled efforts of any church can make a Christian out of a lost man. But once the "great 4, will be transaction's done the communion of believers
found to be the best environment for the new life. Men are made for each other, and this is never more apparent than in the church.

All else being equal, the individual Christian will find in the communion of a local church the most perfect atmosphere for the fullest development of his spiritual life. There also he will find the best arena for the harvest exercise of those gifts and powers with which God may have endowed him.

The religious solitary may gain on a few points, and he may escape some of the irritations of the crowd, but he is a half-man, nevertheless, and worse, he is a half-Christian. Circumstances may for a time compel a man to go on his way alone, but such a situation is to be considered as an emergency and one which should be remedied as soon as possible. Every solitary experience, if we would realize its beneficial effects, should be followed immediately by a return to our own company. There will be found the faith of Christ in its most perfect present manifestation.

But one thing must be kept in mind: these things are true only where the local church is a church indeed. where the communion of saints is more thana phrase from the Creed but is realized and practiced in faith and love. Those religio-social institutions, with which we are all too familiar, where worship is a form, the sermon an essay and the prayer an embarrassed address to someone who isn't there, certainly do not qualify as churches under any scriptural terms with which we are acquainted.

The elements of a true church are few and easy to possess. They area company of believers, the Lord, the Spirit and the Word of the Living God. Let the Lord be worshiped, the Spirit be obeyed, the Word be expounded and followed as the only rule for faith and conduct, and the power of God will begin to show itself as it did to Samson in the camp of Dan.

The church will produce a spiritual culture all its own, wholly unlike anything created by the mind of man and superior to any culture known on earth, ancient or modern. God is getting His people ready for another world, and He uses the local church asa workshop in which to carry on His blessed work.

That Christian is a happy one who has found a coin-pany of true believers in whose heavenly fellowship he can live and love and labor. And nothing else on earth should be as dear to him nor command from him such a degree of loyalty and devotion.

I have seen in autumn a tree shed its leaves, and yet somewhere, on some branch or twig. two or three leaves will stick fast. There one has seen them remain all winter. Springtime comes, a new life awakes, the sap begins to push its way upward to the branches and twigs-then these leaves drop off. They could withstand death; they cannot stand before life. And so with us, old inveterate habits cling to us. We try to get rid of them. Perhaps we groan and sigh, "Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" And no answer seems to come; mortification does not seem to touch them. But let the life and power of the Holy Ghost fill our soul, and 10, they are gone! Death cannot stand before life. So it is that the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus makes us free from the law of sin and death.-Selected.

chapters.t: be done, not corner by corner, but…
p: be done, not corner by corner, but asa whole.

The tobacco firms have their agents in the most distant places. Millions of cigarettes are given away to create new appetites. Do you mean to say that the reason is that there is no longer any demand at home? Of course not. The demand here-especially since women have stepped down from the high pedestal upon which they once stood and have taken to cigarette smoking-is greater than ever. Yet the tobacco firms are already sending their missionaries into foreign lands. They want new markets. In this they are wise than we. It has never been God's will that we should remain at home until the work here is finished. He wants us to go to the entire world, to work the whole field simultaneously.

Do you know what you are saying when you say you do not believe in missions? You are saying that Paul made a mistake; that he should have left your forefathers in Europe to remain pagans; that it would have been better if he had stayed at home in Palestine so that you might have remained in heathenism. Is that what you think? Are you sorry you are not still a heathen? You must be, if you do not believe in missions.
Do you remember when the Lord Jesus Christ fed the five thousand? Do you recall how He had them sit down, row upon row, on the green grass? Then do you remember how Editor: A. W. TozER Looking Ahead
A series Of articles analyzing religious trends.
"Mighty India"

He took the loaves and fishes and blessed them and then broke them and gave them to His disciples? And do you remember how the disciples started at one end of the front row and went right along that front row giving everyone a helping? Then do you recall how they turned right around and started back along that front row again, asking everyone to take a second helping? Do you remember?

No! A thousand times, no! Had they done that, those in the back rows would have risen up and protested most vigorously. "Here,“they would have said.”Come back here. Give usa helping. We have not had any yet. We are starving: it isn't right; it isn't fair. Why should those people in the front rows have a second helping before we in the back rows have had a first?"

And they would have been right. We talk about the second blessing. They have not had the first blessing yet. We talk about the second corning of Christ. They have not heard about the first coming yet. It isn ' t fair. " Why should anyone hear the gospel twice, before everyone has heard it once?" You know, as well as I do, that not one individual in that entire company of five thousand men, besides women and children, got a second helping until every one had had a first helping.

I have never known a minister to have any trouble with the back rows. All his trouble comes from the front rows. Those in the front rows are overfed and they develop spiritual indigestion. They tell him how much to feed them; how long to feed them; what kind of food to give them, and if he does not do it, they complain and find fault. The wise minister would do well to leave the front rows for a while and let them get hungry while he went to feed the back rows. Perhaps when he returned they would be ready to accept his ministry and there would be no murmuring or complaining.

My friends, I have been with the back rows. I have seen the countless millions in those back rows famishing for the Bread of Life. Is it right? Should we be concentrating on the front rows? Ought we not rather to be training the front rows to share what they have with the back rows, and thus reach with the gospel those for whom nothing has been prepared?

Do you know that the greatest thing a church can do for itself is to send its pastor to one of the foreign mission Belds? There is no vacation like it, He will come back a new man; for no one can see the need with his own eyes and ever be the same again. It will do something to him. He will have something to talk about. He will be worth infinitely more to the church than he ever was before. I suggest it because I know what it did for me, and I would recommend that churches everywhere realize its importance and do it. Let him see the back rows. Let him see them for himself. Let him see them waiting in darkness and in midnight gloom for the gospel of Christ.

It costs much to obtain the potter of the Spirit. It costs self-surrender and humiliation and the Yielding up of the most precious things to God. It costs tile perseverance of long waiting and the faith of strong trust. But when ice are really in that power ice shall lind this difference, that whereas before it was hard for us to do the easiest things, note it is easy for us to do the hardest things.

James Here, the friend of the Wesleus at Oxford, describes the change which took place in him through his anointing by the Spirit: that thine his preaching was once like the # ring of an arrow, all the speed and force thereof depending on the strength of his arm in bending the bow, now it was like firing a rifle- ball, the whole force depend ing upon the power back of the ball, and needing oul!, a finger touch to let it of.-A. J. Jordan,

chapters.t: Report on Our Times the Law of Ebb and Flow
p: The history of civilization reveals that the creative powers of the race have not moved uniformly through the years, but fitfully, rather, and unevenly, like the flow of some eccentric fountain. There have been periods when some mysterious Hood-gates were opened within the human soul and from the deep hidden springs of life there came outpourings of great poetry, of noble philosophy, of immortal music, of inspired art and lofty architectural forms which became the established criteria for generations to come. Then the flow of creative energy subsided for a century ora millennium, leaving only imitators to copy monotonously the original work done by the inspired men who had preceded then.

This Rowering of the human mind at certain seasons is a phenomenon which, so far as I know, has never been satisfactorily explained. But that these seasons have come and gone at intervals through the centuries is attested by our habit of breaking up history into ages, as, for instance, the Age of Pericles, the Elizabethan Age and the Victorian Age. These divisions are not arbitrary. They are markers showing where for a brief time a sweet well of water Howed in the desert of human thought. Each brief period was marked by a burst of creative activity in one or another field of human thought and endeavor.

It might prove to be an interesting and profitable bit of research to locate the productive periods in history and compare them with the periods that were relatively sterile, to discover just how they would compare in duration. I venture to guess that the total elapsed time of human cultural fertility would be ~,448%'~ 6. f
found to have been but a short moment in the long reach of the historic past. The genius of the race gives birth only at intervals, and these births are separated by long periods of barrenness.

When the collective mind of the race is in one of its long droughts certain characteristics appear, such as repetition, imitation, and a tendency to split and refine the work of inspired men without doing to the original anything of equal value. After nature has, in a glorious burst of vitality, wrought forth a tree, the literary caterpillars, who are totally incapable of producing anything worth-while themselves, go to work on the leaves, chewing them, rolling them into cocoons or depositing their diminutive eggs under their protecting surfaces.

In the fields of literature, art and music, another characteristic may be noted: Certain would-be geniuses. who for all their ambition to produce are nevertheless barren, in their wild endeavor to bring forth strike out madly in all directions, struggling for originality where nature has obviously never intended that originality should grow. The effects are simply grotesque: Dali-ism in art, bebop in music and gutter-scraping realism in literature. These and their innumerable variations represent the products of uninspired men who seek at any cost to grasp an inspiration which continuously eludes them.

Then, of course, there is always the docile imitator who has nothing much in mind, but who meekly follows the forms outlined for him by the great minds of the past. He dutifully looks at the right pictures, reads the right books and listens to the right music, and should he chance to feel the mild stirrings of r ·· ·,·,.,·—re 7.
the creative urge, his best efforts produce nothing but a weak imitation, thinned down and diluted to the point of complete vapidity.

Were this phenomenon confined to the world of intellect there would be no point in discussing it in a magazine dedicated to the interests of the kingdom of God. But the fact here observed is one which has its counterpart in the realm of the spirit. It represents "natural law in the spiritual world as pointedly as anything cited by Drummond.

The Church of God has also had its times of great spiritual productivity, followed by long periods of relative infertility during which little of any lasting value has been produced. There is no intention here to assert that this is as it should be, or that it follows a law from which there is no escape. To be strictly accurate, it is an observed fact rather thana law; it is something with which we have to deal; and possibly it is something for which we will be held accountable in the day of Christ.

I am not a fatalist. I believe in the potentialities of the human soul to change, to break from its bondage and in the power of the Holy Spirit to destroy the inertia in which it may at any time be held. That the Church has allowed herself to be a victim of these periodic cycles of barrenness does not mean that she has had no choice, that she was simply married along by I aws over which she had no control. The rising and falling of her spiritual tempera-hire over the centuries did not follow any preordained divine plan. It did not represent the will of God for her, but merely her failure or success in the realization of that will.
To a large degree every genera659

Hon of Christians can create its own spiritual climate and decide its own fruitfulness or sterility. This it can do by its response to the revealed will of God, by its willingness to pay the price for spiritual power and to suffer the consequences of following the Lord fully.

A study of the workings of God with Israel and the Church reveals that these times of unusual spiritual productivity of which we speak coincided exactly with the appearance of certain unusual men. These men-prophets, reformers, mystics, revivalists - imparted to others the spirit that inspired them, and mighty religious movements resulted, movements which swept on in power and fruitfulness like the coming of spring to the countryside. With their death and the passing of their generation the tide of power gradually subsided till old barren winter settled down once more to chill and freeze the productive powers of religion.

The characteristics which mark both the spring and the winter of religion are so plain that we should have no trouble in locating ourselves and our day. In this series of articles we plan to do just that.

Dr. A, I. Jordan took an English friend to see Niagara Falls. Taking him to the foot of the falls, he said, "There is the greatest unused potter in the world." "Ah, no, m!~ brother, not so. The greatest unused voice in the world is the Holy Spirit of the Living God."

IN THE past we have had men and movements which wrought in brief but glorious ages of spiritual productiveness. One such age came in with the Reformers; another begin with the Moravians. Church history charts others for us. These times (or rather, these men and movements) were like oases in the desert, or like rocks smitten in the wilderness from which issued water sufficient to quench the thirst of millions, and which still supplies such small pools as may yet be found among us.

It has been a long time since Christianity on her journey has come upon a true oasis, a long time since a rock has gushed out with healing water. We are at present forced to subsist upon the stale waters left from the overflow of the past. We trust we are duly grateful for the isolated cisterns which are here and there among us, but they are not to be mistaken for the full-bodied streams which flow so strongly when the Church is at her flood.

The great spiritual movements of the past were marked by five new things: a new moral reformation, a new spiritual direction, a new intpulse to worship, a neto and radiant hymnody and a new body of deuo -tional and theological literature.

Every upsurge of spiritual life such as we have mentioned here was occon]panied by a marked change in the conduct of the persons involved. A moral reformation resulted. This was wrought about usually by the impassioned preaching of some courageous servant of God, or by an awakened interest in the Scriptures, or by both. So great was the change in the lives of Christians that the whole moral tone of communities and cities was improved. While the new impulse of power did not by any means convert everyone, it did at least serve to elevate appreciably the moral level of public behaviour as far as its influence was felt.
The new spiritual direction was given by a sudden downcoming of the Holy Spirit to make the things. 4,.

the Church at Her Flood of Christ real to a new generation. \Vith this came a sense of spiritual assurance, an inward certainty that took the quavering note out of the Church's utterances and made her divinely sure of herself.

From this intensified feeling of Christ's actual Presence among His people arose the new impulse to worship. According to Zinzendorf, this came at the time of the Moravian pentecost as"a sense of the loving near*ness of the Saviour, instantaneously bestowed. A feeling of de lightful awe brooded over the as -seniblies, sometimes heightening the emotions of the worshipers to a point of positive ecstasy.

Such high spiritual feeling natural-Ir found expression in song. Charles Wesley became God's inspired psalmist to catch the genius of the Moravian movement and set it to music. Iii one generation the Alethodist Church sang Wesley's hymns around the world, and after the passing of more thana century they are still being sung in every church in Christendom. We mention this one instance as being comparatively recent. but the same phenomenon has accompanied every new period of productiveness since Pentecost.
The most marked characteristics of that hymnody which springs out of the Church's high productive moments are its joyousrless and its ' L.. r 1.

sense of spontaneity, The revival hymnist may seize upon older hymn forms or he may create new ones for himself, but, whichever he does, one unfailing mark of his work is its 0 originality. The tide of spiritual power which carries the writer along makes him for a time a true psalmist, to catch and interpret for men the joy felt by the Shepherd as He comes home bearing His sheep on His shoulder, And the saints as they sing feel the same radiant joy. It is this which distinguishes true spiritual singing from the best that trained choirs and talented soloists can produce.

Then there is the matter of religious literature. Every golden age of power wrought into being a fresh body of Christian literature. The reformers and prophets who led the revived Church wrote their message for their people, or set down their day by day accounts in private journals (as Wesley and Woolman, for instance), or caught the inner sense of their own lofty experiences and wrote it into precious books of devotion which were circulated widely and treasured by thousands. Such books have fed the hearts of Christians down the long years from the days of Augustine and his Confessions to times and books more recent and more familiar. These books varied with the age in which they were written and the literary tastes of the time in which they appeared, but one thing they all had in common: they were genuine records of true experiences. Their authors were not imitating anyone. They were spiritual originals who wrote with the bold certainty of bona tide prophets of God.

The history of Israel as given in the Old Testament illustrates the thesis we are setting forth. Israel, too, had her high moments of great spiritual power and productiveness followed by decline and relative sterility continuing sometimes over periods of several hundred years. Then would come some judge or 677 prophet or king who would challenge the evil ways and the cold worship of the times and call the people to repentance and reform. After a generation or two of improved spiritual conditions Israel's basic moral sluggishness would assert itself again, and the downward trend would begin once more and go on till almost every trace of the revival had disappeared.

It is illuminating to observe that, with a few exceptions, the great contributions which Israel made to the world were produced during her high moments of spiritual victory. The Law, for instance, was given at the time of the Deliverance when Fifth in a series

chapters.t: When The Pursuit of God Appeared
p: Then The Pursuit of God appeared, it was received by a grateful sector of the Christian public asa modern statement of an eternal search. In this later volume, written by the same author, the deeper implications of this pursuit of God are very ably set forth.

When a man sets himself to the task of redefining the scope of a full surrender of the life to God, he assumes a heavy responsibility. When this task includes the analysis of present day standards of Christian living, especially in the realm of conservative religion, his task becomes staggering. But Jin Tozer has assumed such a gigantic assignment and has produced a marvelous treatise on what it means to be possessed by God.

Essentially the book is a diagnosis of present-day weakness and a prescription for its cure. Mr. Tozer modestly claims no originality in what he presents, but that he is merely restating the convictions of holy men and women of previous generations. But the book is the life and thought of the author. The writings of the spiritually great have been his food. but the creative energy has been. under the anointing of the Spirit of God, his very own. Recognizing the difficulty of streamlining his message to the artificial demands of our day, he says "In my creature impatience I am often caused to wish that there were some way to bring modern Christians into a deeper spiritual life painlessly by short easy lessons; but such wishes are vain. No short cut exists. God has not bowed to our nervous haste nor embraced the methods of our machine age. It is well that we accept the hard truth now: the man tcho would know God must give time to Hint. He must count no time wasted which is spent in the cultivation of His acquaintance. He must give himself to meditation and prayer hours on end. So did the saints of old, the glorious company of the apostles, the goodly fellowship of the prophets and the believing members of the holy Church in all generations. And so must we if we would follow in their train.

In the diagnosis of the pitifully weak and anemic condition of the accepted orthodoxy of our day. Mr. Tozer points out that the gospel has been proclaimed asa "gift“but not asa”shift," which, he says is demanded by the high moral quality shifted from self to Christ in the acceptance of the gift of salvation. By urging men to accept the gift 49 49

without a corresponding shift, in which the life is radically altered, a spurious and counterfeit Christianity has resulted. He asks, "Is it not true that for most of us who call ourselves Christians, there is no real experience? We have substituted theological ideas for an arresting encounter; we are full of religious notions, but our great weakness is that for our hearts, there is no one there. „

His discernment is keen indeed when he distinguishes the popular presentation of the gospel from the true scriptural pattern. He makes this contrast between the old cross and the new: "The old cross slew men; the new cross entertains them. The old cross condemned; the new cross amuses. The old cross de-stroved confidence in the flesh; the new cross encourages it. The old cross wrought tears and blood; the new cross brings laughter. The flesh, smiling and confident, preaches and sings about the cross; before that cross it bows and toward that cross it points with carefully staged his-trionics-but upon that cross it will not die, and the reproach of that cross it stubbornly refuses to bear.

chapters.t: The Bible: the Book of Life
p: The Bible is unique among books, which means simply that no book has been produced just like it.

The Bible is not a book of history, though it contains much history, and all it does contain is authentic; it is not a book of science, though all its pronouncements upon the facts usually falling into the catagory of science are accurate and trustworthy; it is not a book of biography, though its biographical sketches are easily the most inspiring in the world; it is not a book Rf philosophy, though it is the sum of all that is deep and sound philosophy; it is not a book of astronomy, though its references to the sun and the stars rate among the loftiest sayings ever recorded; it is not a book of psychology, though its knowledge of the workings of the human mind astonishes the reader and lays bare his soul; it is not strictly a book of theology, though it is the source of all the true theology this fallen world will ever know.
What, then, is the Bible? It is the Book of Life. "The words that I speak unto you,“said our Lord,”they are spirit, and they are life."

The Bible is a Iife-bringing and a life-giving Book. It is not primarily concerned with any department of human thought for its own sake. If the Bible speaks about the rainbow, it is that we may be reminded of God's covenant of mercy with mankind; if it tells the story of Abraham. it does so that we may learn to know the place of faith in our relation to God; if it points us to the moon and the stars, it is that we may know how frail we are; if it talks about the birds, it is to teach us to trust our heavenly Father without fear or doubting. It tells us about hell not to satisfy our morbid curiosity, but that we may steer our feet far from its terrors; it tells us about heaven that we may be prepared to enter there. It writes the history of human disgrace that we may learn the value of divine grace; it warns in order that it may turn our feet away from the paths that go down to the path of destruction; it rebukes in order that we may see our own faults and be delivered from them.

Volumes could be written in praise of the Holy Bible without using one word too many. President Woodrow Wilson once said that the Bible is a book of such importance that no one unacquainted with it can be said to be an educated man, and no one who is familiar with it can be said to be uneducated. Sir Walter Scott, when he was dying, called for "the book.“A servant inquired which of his thousands of volumes he meant, and the great man replied,”The Bible, of course. For a dying man there can be no other book. Even the skeptic, George Bernard Shaw, during the last years of his life, kept a Bible near him and never traveled without carrying a copy along with him.

We should all have several Bibles: A well-bound reference Bible for study, and a large-print, plain-text Bible for devotional reading. That many at least. And if we can afford it (and we can if we will cut down somewhere else) we should have a good modern translation or two, such as that by Rotherham or Goodspeed. The New Testament can be secured in a large number of translations, such as Weymouth's or Goodspeed's or Moffatt's. We mention only a few. There are dozens of them. Their chief value is to stimulate interest by affording a change of style, and to throw side-lights upon the text of the familiar King James Version.

Money invested in Bibles is money well spent. Time spent in reading the Bible is not likely to be time wasted. The Bible is the supreme gift for friends and loved ones. Words spoken in favor of the Bible are good words, and if they should fall upon the right ears, might prove to be "apples of gold in pictures of silver."
